math_relationship: SVD is the spectral theorem applied to A^T A (and A A^T); singular values of A = sqrt of eigenvalues of A^T A; both diagonalize via orthonormal bases.

Both are Fourier-domain transforms; the characteristic function is the (continuous) Fourier transform of a probability measure, the DFT its finite/discrete analogue; convolution<->pointwise-product property is shared.
An inner product is a symmetric positive-definite bilinear form; same bilinearity axioms, inner product adds symmetry + positive-definiteness.
A random variable is a measurable function from a probability space to R; shares the measurable-map structure (preimages of Borel sets are events).
The convolution theorem (convolution <-> pointwise product in the Fourier domain) specialized to the cyclic/discrete case is exactly circular convolution = inverse-DFT(DFT(a) .* DFT(b)).
Bayes' rule is derived directly from the definition of conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B); both rest on the joint = conditional * marginal identity.
The FFT is an O(N log N) algorithm that computes exactly the DFT (same linear transform / same output); divide-and-conquer factorization of the DFT matrix.
A Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space; identical inner-product structure, Hilbert adds metric completeness.
Circular convolution is computed via the FFT (pointwise product of FFTs then inverse FFT); shares the DFT-diagonalizes-convolution structure.
The convolution theorem is stated in terms of the DFT: DFT(a (*) b) = DFT(a) .* DFT(b); the theorem and the transform share the same Fourier algebra.
A Hilbert space is built on an inner product (complete inner-product space); the inner product induces the norm and geometry of the Hilbert space.

Both are spectral/Fourier-analytic: the spectral theorem decomposes operators over a frequency/eigenvalue spectrum; the characteristic function is the Fourier (frequency) representation of a distribution. Weaker analogy bridge.
